content: 1. Nijs et al. (2013) conducted a randomized controlled trial to evaluate the impact of family-style meals on energy intake and the risk of malnutrition among residents in Dutch nursing homes. The study demonstrated that communal dining settings could positively influence nutritional outcomes in this population. 2. Simmons et al. (2008) investigated the prevention of unintentional weight loss in nursing home residents through a controlled trial focusing on feeding assistance. Their findings highlighted the importance of structured feeding interventions in maintaining body weight and nutritional health in elderly individuals. 3. Persson et al. (2007) explored the effects of nutritional supplementation and dietary advice on geriatric patients at risk of malnutrition. The study underscored the role of tailored nutritional strategies in improving the nutritional status of older adults. 4. Weekes et al. (2009) examined the efficacy of dietary counseling and food fortification in patients with stable chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) through a randomized trial. The results indicated that these interventions could enhance nutritional intake and overall health outcomes in this patient group. 5. Hickson (2006) reviewed the relationship between malnutrition and aging, emphasizing the multifactorial nature of malnutrition in older adults and its significant impact on health and functional status. 6. Abbott et al. (2013) conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to assess the effectiveness of mealtime interventions on nutritional outcomes for elderly individuals in residential care. The findings supported the implementation of targeted mealtime strategies to improve dietary intake and nutritional health. 7. Adebusoye et al. (2012) evaluated the nutritional status of older individuals attending a primary care clinic in Nigeria. The study identified key demographic and health-related factors contributing to malnutrition in this population. 8. Aliabadi et al. (2008) conducted a cross-sectional study to determine the prevalence of malnutrition among free-living elderly individuals in Iran. The research highlighted the need for public health interventions to address nutritional deficiencies in this demographic. 9. Altus et al. (2002) explored the use of family-style meals to enhance participation and communication among individuals with dementia. The study demonstrated that such meal settings could foster social interaction and improve the overall dining experience. 10. Baweja (2008) assessed the nutritional status and associated risk factors in community-dwelling elderly individuals in Western Rajasthan. The findings emphasized the importance of early identification and management of malnutrition in this population. 11. Benati et al. (2001) investigated the impact of an arginine-enriched nutritional solution on pressure ulcer healing in patients with severe cognitive impairment. The study provided evidence for the therapeutic benefits of targeted nutritional supplementation in wound healing. 12. Boulos et al. (2013) conducted the AMEL study, a cross-sectional survey examining aging and malnutrition among elderly Lebanese individuals living in rural areas. The research provided valuable insights into the prevalence and determinants of malnutrition in this population. 13. Boult et al. (2001) performed a randomized clinical trial to evaluate outpatient geriatric assessment and management. The study demonstrated the potential benefits of comprehensive geriatric care in improving health outcomes for older adults. 14. Cereda et al. (2008) found that the Mini Nutritional Assessment (MNA) is a reliable predictor of functional status in institutionalized elderly individuals at risk of malnutrition. This tool was shown to be effective in identifying those in need of nutritional interventions. 15. Chandra and Puri (1985) demonstrated that nutritional support enhances the antibody response to the influenza virus vaccine in elderly individuals, highlighting the critical role of nutrition in immune function. 16. Charras and Fremontier (2010) conducted a natural experiment to assess the effects of shared meals on institutionalized individuals with dementia. The study revealed that shared dining experiences could improve social engagement and meal satisfaction. 17. Cheserek et al. (2012) examined the nutritional vulnerability of older adults living in urban areas of the Lake Victoria Basin in East Africa. The cross-sectional survey identified key factors contributing to malnutrition in this region. 18. Chilima and Ismail (1998) analyzed the anthropometric characteristics of older adults in rural Malawi, providing baseline data on nutritional status and its implications for health. 19. Chin et al. (2002) conducted a randomized controlled trial to compare the effects of physical exercise and micronutrient supplementation on the well-being of frail elderly individuals. The study highlighted the complementary benefits of these interventions in improving health outcomes. 20. De Castro and Brewer (1992) observed that the amount of food consumed during meals is influenced by the number of people present, suggesting a social component to dietary intake. 21. De Marchi et al. (2008) investigated the association between oral health status and nutritional status in independent-living older adults in southern Brazil. The study emphasized the interrelationship between dental health and nutrition. 22. Elia et al. (2005) discussed the importance of screening for adult malnutrition, advocating for systematic approaches to identify and address nutritional deficiencies. 23. Fulkerson et al. (2014) reviewed the associations between family or shared meal frequency and dietary and weight status outcomes across the lifespan. The findings supported the role of shared meals in promoting healthier eating behaviors. 24. Gündüz et al. (2015) conducted a multicenter, cross-sectional study to assess malnutrition prevalence among community-dwelling elderly individuals in Turkey. The research identified key risk factors and highlighted the need for targeted interventions. 25. Kabir et al. (2006) used the Mini Nutritional Assessment to evaluate the nutritional status of rural elderly individuals in Bangladesh. The study examined the impact of demographic, socioeconomic, and health factors on malnutrition. 26. Keller et al. (2004) demonstrated that nutritional risk predicts quality of life in elderly community-dwelling Canadians, emphasizing the importance of early nutritional assessment and intervention. 27. Keller et al. (2015) proposed a research agenda to improve food and fluid intake for older adults in long-term care settings, focusing on practical strategies to enhance nutritional health. 28. Kwon et al. (2015) evaluated the effects of combined physical training and nutrition interventions on physical performance and health-related quality of life in prefrail older women. The randomized controlled trial demonstrated significant improvements in these outcomes. 29. Liu et al. (2015) conducted a systematic review to optimize eating performance in older adults with dementia living in long-term care. The findings highlighted effective strategies to support nutritional intake in this population. 30. Liu et al. (2014) showed that comprehensive care improves physical recovery in hip-fractured elderly Taiwanese patients with poor nutritional status. The study emphasized the importance of integrated care approaches. 31. Locher et al. (2005) examined the effect of social presence on caloric intake in homebound older adults. The study found that eating with others positively influenced dietary intake. 32. Locher et al. (2007) investigated the relationship between body mass index, weight loss, and mortality in community-dwelling older adults. The findings underscored the health risks associated with unintentional weight loss. 33. Locher et al. (2013) conducted a randomized controlled trial of a behavioral nutrition intervention for community elders. The study provided insights into effective strategies for promoting healthy eating behaviors. 34. Mahadevan et al. (2014) explored the mealtime experiences of assisted-living elderly individuals, identifying factors that influence meal satisfaction and nutritional intake. 35. Margetts et al. (2003) reported that the prevalence of undernutrition risk is associated with poor health status in older adults in the UK, highlighting the need for targeted nutritional interventions. 36. Milne et al. (2009) reviewed the effects of protein and energy supplementation in elderly individuals at risk of malnutrition. The Cochrane review supported the use of supplementation to improve nutritional outcomes. 37. Payette (2002) evaluated the efficacy of nutritional interventions in free-living frail elderly individuals, demonstrating the potential benefits of targeted nutritional support. 38. Pivi et al. (2011) conducted a prospective study on the impact of nutrition education and oral nutritional supplementation in patients with Alzheimer’s disease. The study highlighted the role of nutrition in managing cognitive decline. 39. Ramic et al. (2011) examined the effect of loneliness on malnutrition in the elderly population, emphasizing the psychosocial factors contributing to nutritional health. 40. Rosendahl et al. (2006) evaluated the effects of a high-intensity functional exercise program and protein-enriched energy supplements on older adults dependent on daily living activities. The randomized controlled trial demonstrated significant improvements in physical function and nutritional status. 41. Shahar et al. (2001) investigated the impact of widowhood on weight change, dietary intake, and eating behavior in the elderly population. The study highlighted the emotional and social factors influencing nutrition. 42. Sharkey et al. (2004) identified nutrient intake and body mass index as predictors of the severity of disability in activities of daily living among homebound older adults. The study emphasized the importance of maintaining adequate nutrition. 43. Vedantam et al. (2010) assessed the prevalence and risk factors of malnutrition in free-living elderly individuals in rural South India. The findings highlighted the need for community-based nutritional interventions. 44. Vucea et al. (2014) reviewed interventions aimed at improving mealtime experiences in long-term care settings. The study provided evidence for strategies to enhance the dining environment and nutritional intake. 45. Wouters-Wesseling et al. (2005) evaluated the effect of an enriched drink on cognitive function in frail elderly individuals. The study demonstrated the potential cognitive benefits of targeted nutritional supplementation.
